column2: For the coward without courage who comes down from Bhrigu again, there is the sin of killing a brahmin at every step, no doubt.
A mortal does not live long; why then does he fear death? No one can protect one who has come under the sway of time and death.
That man is most sinful, of wicked conduct, a chandala reviled by the world, who, having taken up renunciation and the like, falls from it.
On seeing a brahmin fallen from renunciation, one should with every effort bathe and look at the sun; for touching him the chandrayana is prescribed.
One should never speak true or false with him, and should remain silent; otherwise one incurs sin.
When death is certain and has come, how can death be ignored? Old age, death and diseases are the flood of the ocean of worldly existence.
Knowing this, best of kings, one should climb the Bhrigu mountain. This I have told you, O king, the excellent greatness of Bhrigu.
One should not tell it to the evil-minded in the Kali age who practise heresy, especially to naked ascetics, white-robed ones, Buddhists and the like.
The wicked who revile the Puranas and Smritis are not to be spoken with; one should never hold conversation with them.
The bull-bannered one himself said to each of the gods: "Those deluded ones who do not accept the king of holy places declared by me,
and those who come down from Bhrigu, go to dreadful hell."
This is the measure of the Kali age, by the measure of its twilight and twilight-portion. Cows give little milk and the earth little grain;
clouds give little water and brahmins have little learning; when the sixteenth year is complete, men have grey hair in youth;
in her tenth or twelfth year a woman conceives; in the Kali age shudras are always devoted to dharma, and there are naked ascetics;
all people will be of one class, and the king will be a barbarian, when the Kali age has come and Madhava is in the form of Kali.
There will be no agnihotra, no Vedas, no dharma and no sacrificing for others; no truth, no austerity, no giving, no goodness and no gods.
Brahmins will sell the Veda in the houses of outcastes, house after house; causing the ruin of the Veda, they will give out the Veda for hire.
Sinners will sell their daughters and live on their daughters. Not a thousandth part of dharma, only a single fraction, will continue.
Wherever there is a siddha, there is a holy place, and men will bathe in the water; house after house, the wives of the twice-born will be shudra women.
In the Kali age men will be with the lower above and the higher below; Buddhists and kshapanakas, sinful, naked, filthy and impure,
deluded, will mock the children of those of sinful deeds; the disciple will not respect the guru, nor the son the father.
Wearing the garb of renunciation, they will steal the wealth of their own families; sinners will live by the emblem and by ash.
When the Vaivasvata Manvantara has come, all this will be in the Kali age. This I have told you, O king, whatever will happen in the Kali age.
I shall tell in brief the origin of Omkara and its rite according to rule, as you have asked me, sinless one.
By reciting the praise of this god one is freed from the bonds of worldly existence. O king, uttering and remembering the one syllable "Om,"
whoever departs, leaving the body, goes to the supreme goal. The Gayatri, mother of the Vedas, arose from Omkara too.
In the one-syllabled principle "Om" are Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara; Omkara is the root of the Veda, and the branches of Shruti are established on it;
its fruits, flowers and leaves are Smriti and Agama. As Omkara is recited at the beginning of all learning,
so at the beginning of all the gods is Maheshvara, the first god. The three twilights, the three times and the rest are declared to be in Omkara;
the three fires, the three worlds and the three aims are established in it. Sixty-eight holy places were declared by Shiva to Brahma;
a hundred and one Rudras are declared; at Kedara a hundred and one; Omkara is one more than a hundred.
The excellent linga Omkara has the five Brahmans and five faces. Of all the lingas on earth reaching to the ocean's end,
none has five faces except Omkara, Yudhishthira. When the Svayambhuva Manvantara had come, in the first kalpa, in the Krita age,
the gods, conquered by the danavas, took refuge on the bank of the Narmada, put to flight by the Kankolas, Kalikeyas and Kalakas.
Those gods with Brahma went to the Lord for refuge. Then Brihaspati said to Brahma, O Bharata:
Perform a most fierce ishti that will destroy the danavas. Then Brahma said to the counsellor of the gods:
I have forgotten the mantras out of fear of the danavas. Meanwhile, splitting the seven netherworlds,
uttering "bhur bhuvah svah" preceded by Omkara, O king, a linga rose from the mountain, radiant as the blazing fire of time,
equal to ten million suns, wreathed in garlands of flame, without beginning, middle or end — nothing so supreme had ever been seen.
With the four aims, the four Vedas, the Vedangas and the Nigamas themselves, Shambhu spoke to Brahma, who brings the worlds into being:
And a gentle one too, O Brahma, that brings peace to the worlds — I have given you the Vedas; perform the ishti as you wish.
Then Brahma performed the fierce ishti that destroys the daityas, and then the gentle ishti that brings peace to the worlds.
Then, great king, seeing the terrible ishti, the asuras, shaken with fear of Brahma's curse, went off in the ten directions.
By the power of Omkara all the gods became fearless; then, having worshipped the lord of gods, the gods went to heaven.
Know Omkara, O king, as the great linga that lasts to the end of the kalpa, saluted by gods and asuras, granting desires and liberation.
At the end of the kalpa all the deities merge into that linga. They call Amara Brahma, Hari Siddheshvara,
Pingaleshvara the sun, and Pitrishvara Soma. Where the three Vedas were perfected with their six limbs, pada and krama,
therefore know it as Siddheshvara, granting every success; it is said to be at the top of the mountain, with a crore of lingas.
By worshipping that linga one is honoured in Vishnu's world. In kalpa after kalpa, great king, all the deities perish,
except five lingas, O king — the Markandeya, the Narmada, Avimukta, Kedara, Omkara-Amareshvara,
and likewise Mahakala — such lingas, O Bharata. Whoever rising at dawn recites these five holy lingas
gains the fruit of all holy places and is honoured in Shiva's world. One Kali dwells always pervading at Mahakala;
a crore and a quarter of holy places dwell at Mahakala, O king; the Kaveri stands in Shiva's field together with Shiva's world, O king;
within four kroshas the sin of killing a brahmin does not creep in. The Agneya Siddhalinga stands on its bank,
known as Shivakhyata at that holy place, delight of the Kurus; a man who merely bathes there is not born again in worldly existence.
Insects, birds, moths and the like, men gone into animal births, are freed there from sin, as is Shiva's word.
Whoever performs shraddha there and gives sesame water to the ancestors — his ancestors are satisfied for thousands of crores of ages.
It is declared the divine one among all the lingas here; bathing there, one goes to heaven and does not enter the straits of the womb,
and gaining the fruit of ten million sacrifices, is honoured in Shiva's world. Eight crores of holy places are declared at Kedara, O king;
by seeing, worshipping and touching it men gain the fruit of liberation; when the water of Kedara is drunk there is no rebirth.
For a celibate who, having stayed a day and night, drinks its water, a linga will arise in his belly within six months;
by the mere sight of Kedara one is honoured in Shiva's world. Most holy Varanasi is renowned in the three worlds;
that city is in the atmosphere, outside the mortal world; within five kroshas the sin of killing a brahmin does not creep in.
There are twenty-eight crores of lingas there, O Bharata. Having bathed as prescribed between the Ganga and the Varana,
freed from all sins one rejoices in heaven like a god. The man who gives up his life there meditating on Shiva
uplifts a thousand generations and goes to Shiva's world. The gift given there has no number;
by giving sesame water the ancestors' satisfaction is imperishable. Whoever gives up his life there, helplessly or willingly,
becomes three-eyed, trident in hand, an attendant of Shiva; by touching the Avimukta linga liberation is attained.
Three kalas abide there in the city of Kashi, no doubt; four kalas are remembered at the meeting of the Ganga and the ocean,
where the Ganga enters the ocean with a thousand mouths; by bathing, immersing, drinking, giving pindas and libations,
a man goes there to Shiva's city with his ancestors. The other is Kalarudra, who dwells in the seven netherworlds;
know that god as Hataka, whom men do not see; he is worshipped by gods and daityas and frequented by gods and siddhas.
Gangeshvara is the second, Sagareshvara the third, and Shulapani the fourth — these are the four kalas.
Rudra of five kalas, across the earth to the ocean's end, is none other than Maheshana, Omkara, who takes forms at will,
with the five Brahmans and five faces, endowed with nine Shaktis — Omkara on the bank of the Kalpaga, as Shiva told long ago.
Therefore in the holy world it is worshipped by the three worlds. The western face is Sadya, like conch, jasmine and moon,
from which the Rigveda came forth, and Brahma is its presiding deity; the northern is Vamadeva, yellow and most charming;
know it as the source of the Yajurveda, and Vishnu is its presiding deity; Aghora, of the colour of cloud, stands in the southern quarter;
know it as the source of the Samaveda, its deity the sun and the fire of time; in the east is to be known Tatpurusha, red as saffron,
from which came the fourth, the Atharva, and the waters are its presiding deity; your face Ishana is five-coloured, of great body,
sung in the conclusions of the Shruti, and Soma is its presiding deity; the sixth is called Sadashiva, without parts and free of affliction;
without marks, devoid of signs — knowing it there is liberation, no doubt. This I have told you, O king, the description of Omkara.
Even one with a thousand mouths has no power to tell it; what then of one with one mouth? Having bathed it with water, one should worship it with bilva leaves;
one is honoured in Rudra's world for four thousand years. Whoever gives up his life at the southern form of Omkara
dwells in Maheshvara's city for thousands of crores of years. A temple and a monastery with plaster and bricks,
with paintings at the base, adorned with banners and flags, canopies with little bells, a fine bamboo staff,
rich with five-coloured decoration, one should have made for Omkara. Having bathed it with the five nectars, with sandal, aloe and saffron,
wrapping it with many beautiful garments, with gold, pearls and jewels, one should burn guggulu with ghee,
a bell, a lamp and smokeless arati, mridangas, patahas, flute, vina and song,
trumpets, conches and instruments, bronze cymbals and the like, a fan, a ball, an umbrella, a chowrie and a banner-staff,
gold, food-vessels and the like, houses, villages and towns — whatever it may be, best of kings, one should offer to Omkara.
The fruit of that gift cannot be counted here. At Siddheshvara and Omkara, at eclipses of moon and sun,
one should make it full of banners and garlands; hear the fruit of that merit: as many times as they are waved again by the wind,
for so many thousands of ages one dwells in Shiva's world, O king — thousands of crores of ages and hundreds of crores of ages,
with every desire fulfilled, in the abodes of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. This I have told you, O king, the account of the origin of Omkara;
now hear the hymn to it composed by Brahma.
Anantapalaka, Dhara, Patalesha, Vrishadhvaja, Sadhumra, Shashvata, Sharva, Sarvapinga, Karalavan,
Vishnu, Isha, Mahatma, Sukha, free of death, Shambhu, Vibhu, Ganadhyaksha, Tryaksha and Divaspati,
Samvada, Vivada, Prabhavishnu, Vivardhana — a hundred and one are remembered as the number of the Rudras.
All the hundred and one are established in Omkara. Having made the hymn thus, Brahma, to the god of gods Maheshvara,
prostrating on the ground with eight limbs and circumambulating, remembering the god in his mind, the Grandsire of the worlds stood.
Hearing the hair-raising hymn of the blessed Brahma, the god of gods spoke to Brahma, O Bharata:
I am pleased with you by this divine hymn; choose a boon. I will give it without doubt, though it be hard even for the gods to obtain.
Brahma said: "If you are pleased, lord of gods, if a boon is to be given me, let the worship in the five faces be named Brahma here."
Hara said: "So be it, O Brahma; what you have said is true." From then on there has been worship of dharma for Brahma, O Bharata.
Brahma said: "Brahmins, kshatriyas and vaishyas will recite before you the Raudra hymn of Omkara, always with minds fixed on it;
they will obtain every desire in this world and the next; whatever desire a man desires, he obtains it.
Reciting the hundred and one daily, he goes to heaven." Having said this, Brahma then bowed to Maheshvara,
mounted a divine vehicle and went joyfully to Brahma's world. A day of Brahma is declared to be a thousand cycles of four ages;
by this very measure Brahma lives a hundred years. A hundred Grandsires make the measure of Vishnu;
in half a blink of Omkara fourteen thousand perish; beyond them, Vishnus, and Grandsires beyond counting.
Knowing thus the course of Brahma, one should always worship Shiva within; Shiva's command abides in the linga, therefore one should always worship the linga.
Whoever out of delusion hates the linga, saluted by all gods, goes to dreadful hell, as is Shiva's word.
Buddhists, kshapanakas and heretics, skilled in false doctrines, lost and destroyed, devoid of the worship of Shiva,
through the habit of birth after birth go to Rasatala. Having thus contended with the Puranas, one should practise the dharma taught by Shiva;
whoever, wicked and sinful of mind, practises another dharma... This I have told you, O king, the Purana proclaimed by Skanda;
by hearing and reciting it one is honoured in Shiva's world.
When the Svayambhuva Manvantara had come, arising from boons obtained from Brahma — Rudravarta, Brahmavarta and Suryavarta as well —
these three are again to be known at the meeting of the Kapila and Narmada, where the Narmada is split, four cubits in measure.
O king, two whirlpools of the Reva and Kapila are remembered there; the Pippalavahini flows there, dwelling in the seven netherworlds.
There too are Kapilavarta and Pippalavarta; the ancestors long for this holy place, which gives them satisfaction.
Therefore a son should carefully, according to rule, give the ancestors a handful of water mixed with sesame and a pinda with effort.
A man delivers his ancestors from the dreadful by performing shraddha. A man who, pure, bathes at the meeting of the Reva and Kapila
and sees Amara there gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. Especially at eclipses of moon and sun and on festival days,
one should offer fragrance, incense, food and a row of lamps; whoever worships the linga with sesame and rice mixed,
anointing it with saffron and wrapping it in red cloths, performing worship with garlands of flowers, gold, jewels and the like —
as long as the moon, the sun, the Himalaya and the great ocean endure, for so many thousands of ages he is honoured in Rudra's world.
Silk, fine silk thread, cotton, red threads, a victory banner and a canopy — one should raise them above the pot,
with the five gems and the tinkling of little bells; as many muhurtas as the number of its threads, O Bharata,
so long one dwells in heaven in the city of Uma and Maheshvara. Another, Ishana, was mentioned earlier in general;
it stands on the eastern side of the Kapila, not far off; by worshipping that linga one attains the leadership of ganas.
On the bright eighth of Kartika the fruit is a hundredfold greater; at the solar transit and at vyatipata it has no number.
By offering gifts and worshipping Kapileshvara one sports in the world of the sun for fifteen thousand years.
A woman whose children die, who is barren, or who miscarries should bathe there with red garments and the five gems
on the fourteenth and eighth in the Kapila, Yudhishthira; she becomes fortunate, with living sons — this truth was spoken by Shiva.
And Uma graciously gave a boon to women. Since the Kapila came forth and flows into the Narmada,
eight thousand holy places granting the fruits of desire and enjoyment abide there, great king, as Shiva said long ago.
Then a tawny cow adorned with every ornament should be given, and brahmins fed there according to one's means,
always intent on fasting; the ancestors and gods are satisfied. The linga named Hemajaleshvara is there, granting success;
by worshipping that god one does not see Yama's world. Vasudana and Dhundhumara were emperors long ago;
by the greatness of this holy place they attained divinity in heaven. Many thousands have attained the supreme perfection —
kshatriyas, best of kings, by the power of Kotitirtha. Where the heads of crows, struck down by owls at Kotitirtha,
fell into the water by the hundreds and thousands, those crows at once had divine bodies and mounted vehicles;
I saw them long ago as kings of the vidyadharas, sinless one. And packs of jackals, for fear of tigers,
entered the water of the Narmada when the sky was covered with clouds; they reached the world of the yakshas, where all desires bear fruit.
Thus it is Jambukeshvara, which frees from animal births. On earth the holy place is Naimisha, in the atmosphere Pushkara,
Varanasi and Prayaga, and in the three worlds Amareshvara, saluted by gods and asuras with thirty-three crores.
Bathing there, king of kings, one gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice; Sarasvati was perfected there by the power of this holy place.
Whoever performs shraddha there, increasing the ancestors' delight, goes to the supreme place together with his ancestors.
The linga named Sarasvata removes the sin of killing a brahmin. I shall tell a story, an ancient history.
When the Svayambhuva Manvantara had come, in the first kalpa, in the Krita age, there was a glorious lord of Ayodhya, valorous as Shakra,
renowned as Dhundhumara, truthful, self-controlled, a performer of sacrifices, generous, a worshipper of gods and guests.
His subjects were blameless, free of fear and poverty; the people lived a hundred and twenty-five thousand years, O Bharata,
with sacrifices, festivals and weddings and the sound of Vedic blessings; the cow of plenty yielded of herself and the earth was rich in crops.
Other common people lived four thousand years; fine silk was tied on the trees everywhere, O Bharata;
with thousands of sacrifices and fire offerings the earth was ever yielding, O king. Thus he ruled the earth as Shakra rules heaven.
Once the king said to his chamberlain: "Summon all the kings born in various lands."
Summoned by the chamberlain, the kings came; with all of them he went to the Vindhya to hunt.
Resounding with the Vedic recitation of brahmins who keep the agnihotra, the Kalpaga of seven kalpas is renowned in the three worlds.
There was a lovely, wondrous circle of forest adorned; having killed thousands of creatures with the kshatriyas, O Bharata,
he entered the whole forest, most dreadful beyond; and there was a terrible form, very fearsome, hard to look at and hard to bear,
roaring with the sound of thunder, most hair-raising — a white boar, dreadful with a pair of tusks.
Seeing such a boar there, the best of kings said to all the kshatriyas: "Neither seen nor heard by me
is such a hair-raising form of a boar." Having said this, taking up a noose, as he made ready to kill it,
it took on a body of wind and went off, tormented for its life, and entered the water at Kotitirtha, lord of men.
The king, riding his horse, followed behind; as soon as the boar entered the water, lord of the people,
it at once had a divine body and was seated in a vehicle that went at will. The king said to the boar in divine form, "What is this?"
filled with wonder in his heart: "Tell me the truth of this." Hearing his words, the boar bearing a divine form
said with a laugh: "Listen, great-minded king: know me as a gana of Shankara named Angada.
Once, as Maheshvara was sporting with the ganas, the chief gods and Uma, before him, best of kings,
I sang there a lovely song in the dandaka style; seeing Urvashi and Rambha, I became bewitched by desire.
I uttered a sow's cry, my voice broken and my face distorted; in my agitation I sported there with the apsarases.
Seeing me thus under the sway of love-play, Nandi, angry at heart, cursed me: 'Become a boar, eater of filth;
for ten thousand years you will wander the earth.' Not even Brahma can undo what is declared of Shiva;
and you, though roaming the earth, are the servant of a servant. Knowing Nandi was angry, I, fearful within,
appeased Nandi, and he declared as a boon the end of the curse: 'By the sight of Dhundhumara and the power of Kotitirtha,
leaving the boar's birth you will come back again.' This I have told you, O king, how I took the birth of a boar,
and how I was freed from the sin by the power of this holy place. By the sight of Omkara, O king, purified by the water of the Reva,
and by your sight, man of good vows, I have attained the birth of a gandharva. Give up despondency, king of kings; the course of karma is deep.
Setting your mind on dharma, be the benefactor of all beings. From birth comes death, O king, and from death arises birth.
Knowing karma as good and bad, uplift yourself. Karma earned by oneself is enjoyed by oneself;
one is oneself the doer and the enjoyer of good and evil alike. Blessings on you; I shall go." Having said this, he went,
an umbrella held over him, fanned by hosts of apsarases, and devoted to meditation on Shiva he dwelt happily on Kailasa.
There was long ago a supremely righteous king named Drumasena, lord of Ayodhya, a mighty emperor.
At the conjunction of Rahu and the sun he went to Kurukshetra, taking elephants, horses, gold and cows,
rubies, diamonds, beryls and garments of many kinds for the brahmins, best of kings, filled with supreme joy.
Having duly given the brahmins seven-storeyed houses perfumed with gold, rich in every desire,
he entreated a brahmin of excellent royal family who lived by gleaning and kept the vow of a prastha of barley meal:
It is the time of my ancestors' shraddha; please take a meal. The sage said: "The sight of a king is dreadful, destroying the intellect, unbearable;
having seen a king one should look at the sun. There is none higher than a brahmin who turns away from receiving gifts;
one who receives an improper gift surely goes to hell. I am one who receives only from his wife; ask another excellent brahmin."
Hearing the sage's words, the king said to his chamberlain: "Let a proclamation be made quickly to the dwellers of Sthaneshvara:
whoever will receive a gift, let him come here quickly." When the proclamation had been made, there was no one who would receive from the king.
Then the king, angry, reproached that place: "This place is without brahmins; there is no Veda and no sacrifice."
Having shown his disgust at them all, he fell silent. Hearing his words, I said to the king:

I am Galava, an eminent brahmin, knower of the four Vedas, of great austerity, a performer of sacrifices, an ascetic, devoted to the good of all beings.
skandapuran:50:21	Know this as a favour: I will lift you from the ocean of existence. The king said: "I will give to you, no doubt; you alone are the best of sages."
Though restrained by all the brahmins headed by Mudgala, sinless one, I took there a horse-chariot adorned with ornaments.
Then Drumasena bowed to me and went, O king. And I, abandoning the agnihotra and other rites, at ease,
enjoyed divine pleasures of many kinds with women, sporting on that account until it was exhausted for me.
Having said this, the brahmin went to the eternal world of Brahma. Then the king, alone, reflected, O Bharata:

If I go alone, on foot, my horse gone, the kings will laugh at me, saying to one another,
skandapuran:50:27	'His horse was killed by robbers,' and the like. Carrying the horse's gear on my head, how can I
skandapuran:50:28	enter the city? This brings me great shame. Until today I have made a brahmin ride.
skandapuran:50:29	For the purification of this sin I shall enter the fire. Having reflected thus, the king there quickly
went south and gathered dry wood; then, kindling the wood and circling it three times,
bowing to the fire, he entered it as if his own house. Overcoming with his radiance the radiance of the fire, the king then —
a four-armed, three-eyed woman adorned with pearl ornaments, taking him by the hand, spoke these words:

Death has not come to you, O king; your time is appointed. This sudden rashness, O god, does not seem fitting to me.
skandapuran:50:34	The Lord himself would not protect a man whose time has come. The king said: "Who are you, fair one — Uma, Ganga or Rama?
Tell me, fortunate one, you who give me devotion." The woman said: "I am not Ganga nor Vani; know me as the Kapila, O king,
who came forth from Rudra and flows beneath the Narmada; at Vasudana's sacrifice arose the confluence of the Reva and Kapila.
Uma, Katyayani, Ganga, Yamuna and Gautami, Sarasvati, Shipra, and the auspicious river Varana,
Shatadru, Chandrabhaga, Sindhu, the pure Reva, Vitasta, the goddess Charmana — from the midst of the Soma concluding bath,
from the waters brought for the bathing of Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesha, from the sesame water of the sages, from the pot water led forth,
and likewise from Soma juice mixed with ghee, sugar and the like, there arose long ago a great overflowing stream born of the sacrifice.
This great holy thing arose and rests on the eastern mountain; the station of Rudravarta is here, best of kings."
Told thus, the king went, and the goddess vanished; the emperor, glad and content, went to Markandeya's hermitage.
Going and bowing to the sage, he sat before him. Markandeya said: "Are you well, best of kings, best of those who know righteous conduct?
Why have you left your army and come here alone?" The king said: "Today my birth is fruitful from seeing your lotus feet."
King Dhundhumara told what had happened before. Then Markandeya, hearing the account of the lord of the earth,
bathed at the meeting of the Reva and Kapila and composed a hymn: "Those who bathe there at the confluence of the Reva and Kapila go to heaven.
Uma, Katyayani, Ganga, Yamuna and Gautami, Sarasvati, Shipra and the auspicious river Varana,
Shatadru, Chandrabhaga, Sindhu, the pure Reva, Vitasta, the goddess Charmana, Bahuda and Varuni,
Sarayu, Gandaki, Gharghara and Badari, Gomati, Venuki, Para and the auspicious Vetravati,
Vipasha, Vaha, Shankhini, Payoshnika, Godavari, Kaveri, Bhima and the auspicious Krishna,
Subhadra, Bhadra, Karatoya and Malini — you are all of these, all-pervading one; I bow to you.
The three worlds are pervaded by you in the form of water, you of good vows; be gracious, fortunate one, purifier of the three worlds."
Hearing this hymn from Markandeya, rich in austerity, the goddess, mounting the Pushpaka vehicle, adorned with every ornament,
four-armed, three-eyed, her face like the orb of the moon, spoke to the great sage Markandeya:
I am pleased by this hymn; choose a boon as you wish. Markandeya said: "If you are well pleased, queen of gods, and wish to give a boon,
take away the impurity of the worlds, auspicious one born of Hara." Bathing and praising in the water, people reached the worlds by Shiva's command.

Give a boon now, goddess, to Dhundhumara; having ruled his kingdom, let him go to heaven with his women and retinue,
skandapuran:50:58	and whatever desire he thinks of, let him obtain it, you of good vows. "So be it, lord of brahmins, whatever you desire of me."
Having said this, the goddess Kapila, purifier of the world, went. The king, bowing to the sage Markandeya, surrounded by sages,
as was fitting, went then to his own city. Then after a long time the king, devoted to dharma,
having ruled and performed sacrifices, Dhundhumara went to heaven. I have told you all this that I saw long ago, sinless one;
by hearing and reciting it one is freed from the bonds of worldly existence.
All this in brief was told as the Purana by Shambhu when Skanda asked; I tell it all to you.
Chandradvipa at Prabhasa, Tamraparni, Gabhastiman, Nagadvipa, Saumya, Gandharva and Varuna,
and the ninth called Kumarika — these are proclaimed the divisions; this earth with its nine divisions has been told to you in brief.
In all these divisions the stream of the Narmada is remembered. Jambu, Shaka, Kusha, Krauncha and Shalmali, Yudhishthira,
Plaksha and Pushkara are proclaimed the seven continents. Salt, milk, curd, ghee, sugarcane juice,
wine and sweet water are proclaimed the seven oceans. Bhurloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka and Maharloka,
Janaloka, Tapoloka, and beyond Satyaloka. Know the space between the earth and the sun, Yudhishthira,
to be four lakh yojanas, the measure of the netherworld too. The Rudras and the eight Vasus dwell here, O Bharata.
I have told you the worlds; learn the netherworlds from me: Atala, Vitala, Sharkara and Gabhastika,
Mahatala, Sutala, then Rasatala, and know the eighth, Sauvarna, endowed with every desire.
The burning of fire, the coolness of water, the blowing of winds, the hardness of the earth and the hollowness of the sky —
this is the very nature of the elements; according to their own natures beings go to their nature; there is no need to deliberate on this.
There are eighty-four lakhs of wombs for those of sinful deeds, and in the dreadful hells the cruel tortures of Yama.
All creatures, confined and led by Yama's servants, experience there many fierce tortures.
Through the fruit of their own karma they obtain good and ill. For this reason austerity, fire offering, giving and meditation purify,
as do compassion to all beings and taking refuge in the Narmada, praise and worship of the Reva, like the rising of the sun.
I shall tell a story as it happened long ago, the dialogue of Muchukunda, the lord of danavas, O Bharata.
There was in the Krita age, O king, in the Chakshusha Manvantara, the royal sage Kuvalayashva, an emperor of great fame.
The kingdom of that king of boundless radiance was eight times Shakra's; many thousands of gifts of many kinds
were given by that king at all the unsurpassed holy places, and sacrifices performed — except at the Kalpaga.
The danava Muchukunda was devoted to all dharma, devoted to brahmins, a devotee of Shiva and of Vishnu, self-controlled.
At the conjunction of Rahu and Soma, on Vaidurya, the mountain of the perfected, where the river Kalpaga dwells together with Omkaranatha —
all the other lingas in the world of moving and unmoving merge at the end of the kalpa into Omkara, no doubt;
this was told by Shiva to Vishnu, to Shatakratu, to Parvati and Shanmukha, in the Purana proclaimed by Skanda —
the lord of men came to the goddess Kalpaga at Kotitirtha, at the meeting of the Narmada and Kapila, furnished with all materials,
taking one lakh milch cows, O king, ten thousand horses and a thousand elephants,
a thousand vehicles that go at will with golden garlands, wealth, grain, garments and jewels of many kinds.
Having bathed as is proper, he then gave to the brahmins, and gave fees too at the southern form of Omkara, lord of men;
whatever desire anyone desired, he gave it to him. King Kuvalayashva, devoted to dharma and rites,
went at the conjunction of Rahu and the sun to Kurukshetra, they say, the lord of Ayodhya himself with his women and retinue,
surrounded by thousands of princes, wishing to bathe; one lakh horses and ten thousand elephants,
gold, rubies, jewels and garments of many kinds, filled with supreme faith, he gave to brahmins, O king.
The rest was distributed in the field, preceded by gifts of sweets. Then, when time had passed, by the power of Kurukshetra,
with thousands of vehicles of many kinds, with his women and retinue, an umbrella held over him, fanned by hosts of apsarases,
to the sound of conches and instruments, adorned with many ornaments, he roamed about there like another vidyadhara.
Muchukunda too, lord of daityas, endowed with every desire, with great vehicles that went at will, adorned with gold and jewels —
hearing thousands of instruments, Dharmaraja, lord of the people, was filled with great wonder and said, "What is this?"
Then Kuvalayashva too, on that day, to that city — both were announced by messengers to the wise Dharmaraja:
The royal sage Kuvalayashva and the mighty Muchukunda — these two have come to the other world, seated in celestial chariots.
Then Muchukunda's vehicle rose up, standing a thousand yojanas above,
while the vehicle of the lord of Ayodhya stood below. Dharmaraja asked Chitragupta the scribe:
Which vehicle shall I approach and honour with arghya and foot-water? He asked the seven sages, chief of sages, judges of dharma and adharma.
Chitragupta said, and the seven sages said: "Approach Muchukunda and honour him with arghya and foot-water.
By the gift at the Kapila, the lord of danavas is to be honoured, and not the other; Kuvalayashva is below and Muchukunda above."
Told thus, Dharmaraja approached the lord of danavas, clad in white garments, adorned with blazing earrings,
and folding his hands stood before the vehicle: "Are you well today, lord of daityas, best of upholders of all dharma?
The three worlds have been won by you through this gift, man of good vows; at the end of the south of Omkara, at the form at the Kapila confluence,
on the bank of her who flows through seven kalpas, gifts have no number." Muchukunda said: "In dharma and adharma you alone today are the bolt of heaven's door."
Addressed thus by the great-souled lord of daityas, Yama there showed the path to the lord of daityas, Yudhishthira.
Then, sent on by him, Muchukunda went, filled with supreme joy, to the city of Uma and Maheshvara.
Having duly sent off the lord of daityas, the king of dharma then approached Kuvalayashva and said:
Welcome to you, great king; may you always be well. Kuvalayashva said: "Gods and danavas are always opposed to each other;
yet passing me by, you honoured the lord of danavas with foot-water and arghya. How have you done all this in reverse, Dharmaraja?"
Yama said: "Give up despondency, king of kings; the course of karma is deep. I am not the giver or taker of the fruit of good and evil;
I am the witness of the karma of all gods, asuras and men, O king. You gave gifts at the Sarasvati at Kurukshetra, sinless one;
but at the end of the Dvapara, gifts elsewhere are not equal to gifts at the Reva — so Shiva told Brahma, Vishnu and the hosts of Maruts.
Holy places are never equal to a fraction of the Kalpaga; I have not spoken falsely — the Purana accords with the Shruti."
Meanwhile, O king, as the two were conversing, Kuvalayashva was addressed by a voice from the sky itself:
Such is dharma, great king; do not make it otherwise in any way; touched by the water of the Kalpaga, the daitya attained Shiva.
The king, filled with wonder, turned back and came again, wishing to bathe in the Narmada at the confluence of the Kapila.
Having bathed there, the king then went to Shiva's world.
Therefore the gift of food is greatly meritorious, O Bharata; the giver of food is called the giver of life; therefore one should be a giver of food.
